metadata.title: SUMMARY OF CDC STI TREATMENT GUIDELINES 2021
metadata.summary: This adaptation of the 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines summarizes recommended and alternative regimens for sexually transmitted infections, primarily those encountered in outpatient practice. It covers treatment for specified patient groups and clinical presentations but does not claim to list every effective regimen.

conditions_covered: First clinical episode of genital herpes
Uncomplicated infections of the cervix, urethra, and rectum
target_population: men who practice insertive anal sex

prophylaxis.recommendation: For recurrent genital herpes in pregnancy, use acyclovir 400 mg orally 3x/day or valacyclovir 500 mg orally 2x/day.
prophylaxis.target_population: Pregnant women with recurrent genital herpes

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use of latex or rubber products, including condoms and diaphragms, within 72 hours after clindamycin ovules treatment is not recommended because the ovules’ oleaginous base might weaken these products.
Use of a cryoprobe in the vagina is not recommended because it poses a risk of vaginal perforation and fistula formation.
prophylaxis.target_population: Persons undergoing treatment for vaginal warts

infection_management.management: For adults and adolescents, use doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; alternatives are azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose or levofloxacin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 7 days. During pregnancy, use azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose; amoxicillin 500 mg orally 3x/day for 7 days is an alternative.

infection_management.prevention: Daily suppressive treatment of recurrent genital herpes in pregnant women is recommended starting at 36 weeks’ gestation.
infection_management.management: For a first clinical episode, use acyclovir 400 mg orally 3x/day for 7–10 days, famciclovir 250 mg orally 3x/day for 7–10 days, or valacyclovir 1 gm orally 2x/day for 7–10 days; treatment can be extended if healing remains incomplete after 10 days. For suppression of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2), use acyclovir 400 mg orally 2x/day, valacyclovir 500 mg orally 1x/day, valacyclovir 1 gm orally 1x/day, or famciclovir 250 mg orally 2x/day. Valacyclovir 500 mg once a day might be less effective than other valacyclovir or acyclovir dosing regimens when recurrences are frequent (≥10 episodes/year). For episodic treatment of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2), use acyclovir 800 mg orally 2x/day for 5 days or 3x/day for 2 days; famciclovir 1 gm orally 2x/day for 1 day, 500 mg once followed by 250 mg 2x/day for 2 days, or 125 mg 2x/day for 5 days; or valacyclovir 500 mg orally 2x/day for 3 days or 1 gm orally 1x/day for 5 days. In persons with HIV infection, daily suppression uses acyclovir 400-800 mg orally 2x–3x/day, famciclovir 500 mg orally 2x/day, or valacyclovir 500 mg orally 2x/day; episodic treatment uses acyclovir 400 mg orally 3x/day for 5–10 days, famciclovir 500 mg orally 2x/day for 5–10 days, or valacyclovir 1 gm orally 2x/day for 5–10 days. During pregnancy, daily suppression uses acyclovir 400 mg orally 3x/day or valacyclovir 500 mg orally 2x/day.

For uncomplicated cervical, urethral, or rectal infection in adults and adolescents weighing <150 kg, use ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose. With cephalosporin allergy, the listed alternative is gentamicin 240 mg IM in a single dose plus azithromycin 2 gm orally in a single dose; if ceftriaxone cannot feasibly be administered, the listed alternative is cefixime 800 mg orally in a single dose. For uncomplicated pharyngeal infection in adults and adolescents weighing <150 kg, and for infection during pregnancy, use ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose. For persons weighing ≥150 kg, administer 1 gm ceftriaxone. If chlamydial infection has not been excluded, also treat it with doxycycline 100 mg orally two times/day for 7 days, or, during pregnancy, azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose. For conjunctivitis, use ceftriaxone 1 gm IM in a single dose; providers should consider a one-time saline lavage of the infected eye. For disseminated gonococcal infections (DGI), use ceftriaxone 1 gm IM or by IV every 24 hours; alternatives are cefotaxime 1 gm by IV every 8 hours or ceftizoxime 1 gm every 8 hours. When treating arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, a provider can switch to an oral agent selected by antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) 24–48 hours after substantial clinical improvement, completing at least 7 days of treatment.

Parenteral options are ceftriaxone 1 gm by IV every 24 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally or by IV every 12 hrs and metronidazole 500 mg orally or by IV every 12 hours; cefotetan 2 gm by IV every 12 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally or by IV every 12 hrs; or cefoxitin 2 gm by IV every 6 hours plus doxycycline 100 mg orally or by IV every 12 hrs. Listed alternatives are ampicillin-sulbactam 3 gm by IV every 6 hrs plus doxycycline 100 mg orally or by IV every 12 hours, or clindamycin 900 mg by IV every 8 hours plus gentamicin 2 mg/kg body weight by IV or IM followed by 1.5 mg/kg body weight every 8 hrs; gentamicin 3–5 mg/kg body weight 1x/day can be substituted. Intramuscular or oral options are ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose, cefoxitin 2 gm IM in a single dose with probenecid 1 gm orally given concurrently in a single dose, or another parenteral third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftizoxime or cefotaxime); each is combined with doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 14 days and metronidazole 500 mg orally 2x/day for 14 days.

For primary, secondary, and early latent syphilis in adults, including pregnant women and people with HIV infection, use benzathine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM in a single dose. For late latent syphilis in these adults, use benzathine penicillin G 7.2 million units total as 3 doses of 2.4 million units IM each at 1-week intervals. For neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, or otosyphilis, use aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units per day, given as 3–4 million units by IV every 4 hours or by continuous infusion for 10–14 days; the listed alternative is procaine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM 1x/day plus probenecid 500 mg orally 4x/day, both for 10–14 days. For children or congenital syphilis, the document directs readers to Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021.

Recommended options are metronidazole 500 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; metronidazole gel 0.75%, one 5 gm applicator intravaginally 1x/day for 5 days; or clindamycin cream 2%, one 5 gm applicator intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days. Alternatives are clindamycin 300 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; clindamycin ovules 100 mg intravaginally at bedtime for 3 days; secnidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose; tinidazole 2 gm orally 1x/day for 2 days; or tinidazole 1 gm orally 1x/day for 5 days. Before taking secnidazole oral granules, sprinkle them on unsweetened applesauce, yogurt, or pudding; water can be taken afterward to help with swallowing.

Use doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose is an alternative. Consider simultaneous treatment for gonococcal infection if the patient is at risk for gonorrhea or lives where gonorrhea prevalence is high.

For acute epididymitis most likely caused by sexually transmitted chlamydia and gonorrhea, use ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 10 days. If chlamydia, gonorrhea, or enteric organisms are most likely in men who practice insertive anal sex, use ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose plus levofloxacin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 10 days. If enteric organisms alone are most likely, use levofloxacin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 10 days.

For external anogenital warts, patient-applied options are imiquimod 3.75% or 5% cream, podofilox 0.5% solution or gel, or sinecatechins 15% ointment. Provider-administered options are cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen or cryoprobe; surgical removal by tangential scissor excision, tangential shave excision, curettage, laser, or electrosurgery; or trichloroacetic acid (TCA) or bichloroacetic acid (BCA) 80%–90% solution. External anal warts might warrant anal-canal inspection by digital examination, standard anoscopy, or high-resolution anoscopy. For urethral meatus warts, use cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen or surgical removal. For vaginal, cervical, or intra-anal warts, use cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, surgical removal, or TCA or BCA 80%–90% solution. Do not use a cryoprobe in the vagina because of the risk of vaginal perforation and fistula formation. Management of cervical and intra-anal warts should include specialist consultation; before treating exophytic cervical warts, perform a biopsy evaluation to exclude high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion.

Use doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 21 days. Alternatives are azithromycin 1 gm orally 1x/week for 3 weeks or erythromycin base 500 mg orally 4x/day for 21 days. Because the azithromycin regimen has not been rigorously validated, a test-of-cure with Chlamydia trachomatis nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) 4 weeks after treatment can be considered.

Use doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; alternatives are azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose or azithromycin 500 mg orally in a single dose followed by 250 mg 1x/day for 4 days. For persistent or recurrent NGU, test for Mycoplasma genitalium. If M. genitalium is found by an FDA-cleared NAAT but resistance testing is unavailable, give doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg 1x/day for 7 days. If resistance testing is unavailable and moxifloxacin cannot be used, give doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days, then azithromycin 1 gm orally on first day followed by azithromycin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 3 days, with a test-of-cure 21 days after treatment completion. When resistance testing is available, use resistance-guided treatment: for macrolide-sensitive infection, doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days followed by azithromycin 1 gm orally initial dose and azithromycin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 3 additional days (2.5 gm total); for macrolide resistance, doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg orally 1x/day for 7 days. In heterosexual men where Trichomonas vaginalis infection is prevalent, test for it; the listed treatments are metronidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose or tinidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose.

For women, use metronidazole 500 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; tinidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose is an alternative. For men, use metronidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose; tinidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose is an alternative. For persistent or recurrent infection, the document directs readers to Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021.

therapies_index.name: doxycycline
approved_indications: gonococcal infection when chlamydial infection has not been excluded
therapies_index.administration: 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days for Chlamydial Infections, Cervicitis, and Nongonococcal Urethritis (NGU); 100 mg orally 2x/day for 10 days for Epididymitis most likely caused by sexually transmitted chlamydia and gonorrhea; 100 mg orally 2x/day for 14 days in intramuscular or oral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) regimens; 100 mg orally 2x/day for 21 days for Lymphogranuloma Venereum. Parenteral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) regimens give 100 mg orally or by IV every 12 hours or every 12 hrs.

therapies_index.name: azithromycin
approved_indications: gonococcal infection when chlamydial infection has not been excluded in pregnancy
therapies_index.administration: 1 gm orally in a single dose for Chlamydial Infections and Cervicitis, and when treating chlamydia in pregnancy; 1 gm orally 1x/week for 3 weeks for Lymphogranuloma Venereum; for Nongonococcal Urethritis (NGU), either 1 gm orally in a single dose or 500 mg orally in a single dose, THEN 250 mg 1x/day for 4 days. Persistent or Recurrent NGU regimens give 1 gm orally as the first or initial dose, FOLLOWED BY 500 mg orally 1x/day for 3 days or 3 additional days.
monitoring: For the Lymphogranuloma Venereum regimen, a test-of-cure with Chlamydia trachomatis nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) 4 weeks after treatment can be considered because the regimen has not been rigorously validated.

therapies_index.name: levofloxacin
therapies_index.administration: 500 mg orally 1x/day for 7 days for Chlamydial Infections; 500 mg orally 1x/day for 10 days for the specified acute Epididymitis presentations.

therapies_index.name: amoxicillin
therapies_index.administration: 500 mg orally 3x/day for 7 days.

therapies_index.name: acyclovir
approved_indications: First clinical episode of genital herpes
Suppressive therapy for recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2)
Episodic therapy for recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2)
Daily suppressive therapy for persons with HIV infection
Episodic therapy for persons with HIV infection
Daily suppressive therapy of recurrent genital herpes in pregnant women
therapies_index.administration: 400 mg orally 3x/day for 7–10 days for a first clinical episode; 400 mg orally 2x/day for suppression of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2); 800 mg orally 2x/day for 5 days or 800 mg orally 3x/day for 2 days for episodic treatment of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2). For persons with HIV infection, suppression uses 400-800 mg orally 2x–3x/day and episodic treatment uses 400 mg orally 3x/day for 5–10 days. In pregnancy, suppressive treatment uses 400 mg orally 3x/day, starting at 36 weeks’ gestation. The guide also identifies 200 mg orally five times/day for a first episode and 400 mg orally three times/day for recurrent episodic treatment as effective but not recommended because of dosing frequency.

therapies_index.name: famciclovir
approved_indications: First clinical episode of genital herpes
Suppressive therapy for recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2)
Episodic therapy for recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2)
Daily suppressive therapy for persons with HIV infection
Episodic therapy for persons with HIV infection
therapies_index.administration: 250 mg orally 3x/day for 7–10 days for a first episode; 250 mg orally 2x/day for suppression of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2). Episodic regimens for recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2) are 1 gm orally 2x/day for 1 day, 500 mg once FOLLOWED BY 250 mg 2x/day for 2 days, or 125 mg 2x/day for 5 days. For persons with HIV infection, daily suppression uses 500 mg orally 2x/day and episodic treatment uses 500 mg orally 2x/day for 5–10 days.

therapies_index.name: valacyclovir
approved_indications: First clinical episode of genital herpes
Suppressive therapy for recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2)
Episodic therapy for recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2)
Daily suppressive therapy for persons with HIV infection
Episodic therapy for persons with HIV infection
Daily suppressive therapy of recurrent genital herpes in pregnant women
therapies_index.administration: 1 gm orally 2x/day for 7–10 days for a first episode; 500 mg orally 1x/day or 1 gm orally 1x/day for suppression of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2); 500 mg orally 2x/day for 3 days or 1 gm orally 1x/day for 5 days for episodic treatment of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2). For persons with HIV infection, daily suppression uses 500 mg orally 2x/day and episodic treatment uses 1 gm orally 2x/day for 5–10 days. In pregnancy, suppressive treatment uses 500 mg orally 2x/day, starting at 36 weeks’ gestation.

therapies_index.name: ceftriaxone
therapies_index.administration: For uncomplicated gonococcal infection in adults and adolescents <150 kg and for gonococcal infection in pregnancy, 500 mg IM in a single dose; for persons weighing ≥150 kg, 1 gm should be administered. For Conjunctivitis, 1 gm IM in a single dose. For Disseminated gonococcal infections (DGI), 1 gm IM or by IV every 24 hours. For parenteral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), 1 gm by IV every 24 hours. Intramuscular or oral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) regimens and specified Epididymitis regimens use 500 mg IM in a single dose, subject to the guide’s weight-based note.

therapies_index.name: gentamicin
approved_indications: Uncomplicated gonococcal infections when there is cephalosporin allergy
therapies_index.administration: 240 mg IM in a single dose with azithromycin for uncomplicated gonococcal infections when there is cephalosporin allergy. For parenteral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), 2 mg/kg body weight by IV or IM FOLLOWED BY 1.5 mg/kg body weight every 8 hrs; 3–5 mg/kg body weight 1x/day can be substituted.

therapies_index.name: cefixime
approved_indications: Uncomplicated gonococcal infections of the cervix, urethra, and rectum when ceftriaxone administration is not available or not feasible
therapies_index.administration: 800 mg orally in a single dose.

therapies_index.name: cefotaxime
therapies_index.administration: 1 gm by IV every 8 hours as an alternative for Disseminated gonococcal infections (DGI). The guide also names it as an example of another parenteral third-generation cephalosporin in an intramuscular or oral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) regimen, without specifying its dose there.

therapies_index.name: ceftizoxime
therapies_index.administration: 1 gm every 8 hours as an alternative for Disseminated gonococcal infections (DGI). The guide also names it as an example of another parenteral third-generation cephalosporin in an intramuscular or oral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID) regimen, without specifying its dose there.

therapies_index.name: ampicillin-sulbactam
therapies_index.administration: 3 gm by IV every 6 hrs, combined with doxycycline.

therapies_index.name: metronidazole
approved_indications: Trichomonas vaginalis in heterosexual men with Persistent or Recurrent NGU in areas where infection is prevalent
therapies_index.administration: For parenteral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), 500 mg orally or by IV every 12 hours; for intramuscular or oral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID), 500 mg orally 2x/day for 14 days. For Bacterial Vaginosis and Trichomoniasis in women, 500 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days. For Trichomoniasis in men and the specified Trichomonas vaginalis presentation, 2 gm orally in a single dose.

therapies_index.name: clindamycin
therapies_index.administration: 900 mg by IV every 8 hours with gentamicin for parenteral Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID); 300 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days as an alternative for Bacterial Vaginosis.

therapies_index.name: cefotetan
therapies_index.administration: 2 gm by IV every 12 hours with doxycycline.

therapies_index.name: cefoxitin
therapies_index.administration: 2 gm by IV every 6 hours with doxycycline for parenteral treatment; 2 gm IM in a single dose with concurrently administered probenecid, followed by the specified doxycycline and metronidazole regimen for intramuscular or oral treatment.

therapies_index.name: probenecid
therapies_index.administration: 1 gm orally, concurrently with cefoxitin in a single dose for Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID); 500 mg orally 4x/day with procaine penicillin G, both for 10–14 days, for Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, and otosyphilis.

approved_indications: Primary, secondary, and early latent Syphilis in adults, including pregnant women and people with HIV infection

therapies_index.administration: 2.4 million units IM in a single dose for primary, secondary, and early latent Syphilis; 7.2 million units total, administered as 3 doses of 2.4 million units IM each at 1-week intervals, for late latent Syphilis.

therapies_index.administration: 2.4 million units IM 1x/day with probenecid, both for 10–14 days.

therapies_index.name: metronidazole gel
therapies_index.administration: 0.75%, one 5 gm applicator intravaginally, 1x/day for 5 days.

therapies_index.name: clindamycin cream
therapies_index.administration: 2%, one 5 gm applicator intravaginally, at bedtime for 7 days.

therapies_index.name: clindamycin ovules
therapies_index.administration: 100 mg intravaginally at bedtime for 3 days. Their oleaginous base might weaken latex or rubber products; use of those products within 72 hours after treatment is not recommended.

therapies_index.name: secnidazole

therapies_index.name: bichloroacetic acid (BCA)

recommendations.statement: For late latent syphilis in adults, administer benzathine penicillin G 7.2 million units total as 3 doses of 2.4 million units IM each at 1-week intervals.
recommendations.context: Includes pregnant women and people with HIV infection.

recommendations.statement: For neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, or otosyphilis, administer aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18–24 million units per day as 3–4 million units by IV every 4 hours or by continuous infusion for 10–14 days. An alternative is procaine penicillin G 2.4 million units IM 1x/day plus probenecid 500 mg orally 4x/day, both for 10–14 days.
recommendations.context: Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, and otosyphilis

recommendations.statement: For children or congenital syphilis, consult Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021.
recommendations.context: The summary directs readers to the complete guideline for these treatments.

recommendations.statement: Treat with metronidazole 500 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days, metronidazole gel 0.75% using one 5 gm applicator intravaginally 1x/day for 5 days, or clindamycin cream 2% using one 5 gm applicator intravaginally at bedtime for 7 days.
recommendations.context: Recommended regimens

recommendations.statement: Alternative regimens are clindamycin 300 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; clindamycin ovules 100 mg intravaginally at bedtime for 3 days; secnidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose; tinidazole 2 gm orally 1x/day for 2 days; or tinidazole 1 gm orally 1x/day for 5 days.
recommendations.context: Clindamycin ovules might weaken latex or rubber products, so their use within 72 hours after treatment is not recommended. Sprinkle secnidazole oral granules onto unsweetened applesauce, yogurt, or pudding before ingestion; water can be taken afterward to help swallowing.

recommendations.statement: Treat with doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose is an alternative.
recommendations.context: Cervicitis

recommendations.statement: Consider simultaneous treatment for gonococcal infection when the patient is at risk for gonorrhea or lives in a community with high gonorrhea prevalence.
recommendations.context: Cervicitis

recommendations.statement: For acute epididymitis most likely due to sexually transmitted chlamydia and gonorrhea, give ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 10 days.
recommendations.context: The ceftriaxone dose is subject to the document’s ≥150 kg dosing note.

recommendations.statement: For acute epididymitis most likely due to chlamydia, gonorrhea, or enteric organisms in men who practice insertive anal sex, give ceftriaxone 500 mg IM in a single dose plus levofloxacin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 10 days.
recommendations.context: The ceftriaxone dose is subject to the document’s ≥150 kg dosing note.

recommendations.statement: For acute epididymitis most likely due only to enteric organisms, give levofloxacin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 10 days.
recommendations.context: Enteric organisms only

recommendations.statement: For external anogenital warts, patient-applied choices are imiquimod 3.75% or 5% cream, podofilox 0.5% solution or gel, or sinecatechins 15% ointment. Provider-administered choices are cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen or a cryoprobe; surgical removal by tangential scissor excision, tangential shave excision, curettage, laser, or electrosurgery; or trichloroacetic acid (TCA) or bichloroacetic acid (BCA) 80%–90% solution.
recommendations.context: imiquimod and sinecatechins might weaken condoms and vaginal diaphragms.

recommendations.statement: For external anal warts, consider inspecting the anal canal by digital examination, standard anoscopy, or high-resolution anoscopy.
recommendations.context: Persons with external anal or peri-anal warts might also have intra-anal warts.
recommendations.rationale: External anal or peri-anal warts can coexist with intra-anal warts.

recommendations.statement: For urethral meatus warts, use cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen or surgical removal.
recommendations.context: Urethral meatus warts

recommendations.statement: For vaginal, cervical, or intra-anal warts, use cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, surgical removal, or TCA or BCA 80%–90% solution.
recommendations.context: Vaginal warts, cervical warts, and intra-anal warts

recommendations.statement: Use of a cryoprobe in the vagina is not recommended.
recommendations.context: Treatment of vaginal warts
recommendations.rationale: A vaginal cryoprobe carries risks of perforation and fistula formation.

recommendations.statement: Include specialist consultation in the management of cervical warts. Before starting treatment for exophytic cervical warts, perform a biopsy evaluation to exclude high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion.
recommendations.context: Cervical warts

recommendations.statement: Include specialist consultation in the management of intra-anal warts.
recommendations.context: Intra-anal warts

recommendations.statement: Treat with doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 21 days. Alternatives are azithromycin 1 gm orally 1x/week for 3 weeks or erythromycin base 500 mg orally 4x/day for 21 days.
recommendations.context: If azithromycin is used, a test-of-cure with Chlamydia trachomatis nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) 4 weeks after completion of treatment can be considered.
recommendations.rationale: The azithromycin regimen has not been rigorously validated.

recommendations.statement: Treat with doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days. Alternatives are azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose or azithromycin 500 mg orally in a single dose followed by 250 mg 1x/day for 4 days.

recommendations.statement: For persistent or recurrent NGU, test for Mycoplasma genitalium.

recommendations.statement: If M. genitalium is detected by an FDA-cleared NAAT and resistance testing is unavailable, give doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg 1x/day for 7 days.
recommendations.context: Persistent or recurrent NGU without M. genitalium resistance testing

recommendations.statement: When resistance testing is unavailable and moxifloxacin cannot be used, give doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days followed by azithromycin 1 gm orally on the first day and azithromycin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 3 days; perform a test-of-cure 21 days after treatment completion.
recommendations.context: Persistent or recurrent NGU when moxifloxacin cannot be used

recommendations.statement: If resistance testing is available, select treatment according to the resistance result. For macrolide-sensitive infection, give doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days, followed by azithromycin 1 gm orally initially and then azithromycin 500 mg orally 1x/day for 3 additional days (2.5 gm total). For macrolide resistance, give doxycycline 100 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days followed by moxifloxacin 400 mg orally 1x/day for 7 days.
recommendations.context: Persistent or recurrent NGU with M. genitalium resistance testing

recommendations.statement: In heterosexual men in areas where infection is prevalent, test for Trichomonas vaginalis; the listed treatments are metronidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose or tinidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose.
recommendations.context: Persistent or recurrent NGU

recommendations.statement: Treat women with metronidazole 500 mg orally 2x/day for 7 days; tinidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose is an alternative.

recommendations.statement: Treat men with metronidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose; tinidazole 2 gm orally in a single dose is an alternative.

document_sections.heading: SUMMARY OF CDC STI TREATMENT GUIDELINES 2021
document_sections.content: This outpatient-focused treatment summary adapts the 2021 CDC STI Treatment Guidelines. Its regimen tables provide clinical guidance but do not include every effective option. The complete CDC guidelines provide further detail.

document_sections.heading: Chlamydial Infections
document_sections.content: The table distinguishes treatment for adults and adolescents from treatment during pregnancy. For adults and adolescents, it presents doxycycline as the recommended regimen and azithromycin or levofloxacin as alternatives. During pregnancy, it lists azithromycin as recommended and amoxicillin as an alternative.

document_sections.heading: Genital Herpes Simplex
document_sections.content: The table covers the first clinical episode, suppressive and episodic treatment of recurrent genital herpes (HSV-2), treatment for persons with HIV infection, and suppressive treatment during pregnancy. Initial-episode options include acyclovir, famciclovir and valacyclovir; therapy may be extended when healing remains incomplete after 10 days. For recurrent disease, the table gives distinct daily suppressive and episodic schedules. Acyclovir 200 mg orally five times/day is effective but is not recommended because dosing is frequent. For persons with ≥10 episodes/year, valacyclovir 500 mg once a day might be less effective than the other listed valacyclovir or acyclovir schedules. Acyclovir 400 mg orally three times/day is also effective for episodic treatment but is not recommended because of dosing frequency. Separate suppressive and episodic schedules are provided for persons with HIV infection. Suppressive treatment in pregnancy is recommended beginning at 36 weeks’ gestation.

document_sections.heading: Gonococcal Infections
document_sections.content: The table presents treatment for uncomplicated cervical, urethral, rectal and pharyngeal infections in adults and adolescents weighing <150 kg, as well as for pregnancy, conjunctivitis and disseminated gonococcal infections (DGI). It specifies alternatives for cephalosporin allergy, circumstances in which ceftriaxone administration is unavailable or infeasible, and DGI. For persons weighing ≥150 kg, the ceftriaxone dose is 1 gm. If chlamydial infection has not been excluded, add treatment with doxycycline 100 mg orally two times/day for 7 days; during pregnancy, use azithromycin 1 gm orally in a single dose instead. For gonococcal conjunctivitis, clinicians should consider a single saline lavage of the affected eye. When treating arthritis-dermatitis syndrome, an oral agent selected through antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) can replace initial therapy 24–48 hours after substantial clinical improvement, provided the total treatment course lasts at least 7 days.

document_sections.heading: Pelvic Inflammatory Disease (PID)
document_sections.content: The table separates parenteral treatment from intramuscular or oral treatment. Its parenteral options include ceftriaxone with doxycycline and metronidazole, cefotetan or cefoxitin with doxycycline, and alternative combinations using ampicillin-sulbactam with doxycycline or clindamycin with gentamicin. Its intramuscular or oral options pair doxycycline and metronidazole with ceftriaxone, cefoxitin plus probenecid, or another parenteral third-generation cephalosporin. The gentamicin schedule permits substitution with 3–5 mg/kg body weight 1x/day.

document_sections.heading: Syphilis
document_sections.content: The table differentiates primary, secondary and early latent syphilis; late latent syphilis; and neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis. The adult regimens for early and late latent disease explicitly include pregnant women and people with HIV infection. It lists benzathine penicillin G for early and late latent disease, aqueous crystalline penicillin G for neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis and otosyphilis, and procaine penicillin G with probenecid as an alternative for the latter group. For children or congenital syphilis, it directs readers to the complete Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021; that publication also contains the full set of syphilis-treatment recommendations.

document_sections.heading: Bacterial Vaginosis
document_sections.content: The table gives oral and intravaginal metronidazole and intravaginal clindamycin cream as recommended options. Alternatives include oral clindamycin, intravaginal clindamycin ovules, secnidazole and tinidazole. Before taking secnidazole oral granules, they should be placed on unsweetened applesauce, yogurt or pudding; water may then help with swallowing. Because clindamycin ovules have an oily base that might weaken latex or rubber products, use of products such as condoms or diaphragms within 72 hours after treatment is not recommended.

document_sections.heading: Cervicitis
document_sections.content: The table recommends doxycycline and lists azithromycin as an alternative. Concurrent treatment for gonococcal infection should be considered when a patient has gonorrhea risk or lives in a community with high gonorrhea prevalence.

document_sections.heading: Epididymitis
document_sections.content: The table differentiates acute epididymitis most likely due to sexually transmitted chlamydia and gonorrhea, disease potentially involving chlamydia, gonorrhea or enteric organisms in men who practice insertive anal sex, and disease most likely due only to enteric organisms. It lists ceftriaxone with doxycycline for the first group, ceftriaxone with levofloxacin for the second, and levofloxacin alone for the third.

document_sections.heading: Genital Warts (Human Papillomavirus)
document_sections.content: For external anogenital warts, the table distinguishes patient-applied imiquimod, podofilox and sinecatechins from provider-administered cryotherapy, surgical removal and acid treatment. It also gives site-specific options for urethral meatus, vaginal, cervical and intra-anal warts. People with external anal or peri-anal warts might also have intra-anal lesions; examination of the anal canal by digital examination, standard anoscopy or high-resolution anoscopy might therefore be useful. Imiquimod and sinecatechins might weaken condoms and vaginal diaphragms. A vaginal cryoprobe is not recommended because it risks perforation and fistula formation. Management of cervical and intra-anal warts should involve specialist consultation. Before treatment of exophytic cervical warts, biopsy should assess for high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion.

document_sections.heading: Lymphogranuloma Venereum
document_sections.content: The table recommends doxycycline and gives azithromycin and erythromycin base as alternatives. Because the azithromycin schedule has not undergone rigorous validation, a test of cure using Chlamydia trachomatis nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT) can be considered 4 weeks after treatment ends.

document_sections.heading: Nongonococcal Urethritis (NGU)
document_sections.content: The table recommends doxycycline for initial NGU and lists azithromycin schedules as alternatives. For persistent or recurrent NGU, it calls for testing for Mycoplasma genitalium. If an FDA-cleared NAAT detects M. genitalium but resistance testing is unavailable, it lists doxycycline followed by moxifloxacin. When resistance testing is unavailable and moxifloxacin cannot be used, it gives doxycycline followed by azithromycin, with a test of cure 21 days after treatment completion. If resistance testing is available, therapy is guided by its results: the table distinguishes macrolide-sensitive from macrolide-resistant infection. For heterosexual men in areas where Trichomonas vaginalis infection is prevalent, it calls for testing and lists metronidazole or tinidazole treatment.

document_sections.heading: Trichomoniasis
document_sections.content: The table distinguishes treatment for women and men. It recommends a metronidazole schedule specific to each group and lists tinidazole as an alternative for both. For persistent or recurrent infection, it directs readers to the complete Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, 2021.
